summary:
Autumn Solara is an interactive web platform that evaluates and compares 14 terrestrial analog sites against four NASA lunar and Martian destinations: Shackleton Crater, Copernicus Crater, Jezero Crater, and Alba Mons.
Addressing the challenge through open telemetry from LRO (LOLA, Diviner), MGS (MOLA, TES), Mars Odyssey (THEMIS), SRTM, ASTER, and MODIS, the platform dynamically ranks all 14 field sites, including seven new candidates, using a live Planetary Fidelity Index (PFI) across eight scientific dimensions. Users can explore an orbital map with optical, topographic, and thermal layers plus a live coordinate scanner, and test rover mobility on an interactive altimetric transect simulator that calculates pitch, slope stability, and traction power (W) under lunar, Martian, and Earth gravity. Opening any site reveals a full geological case study featuring a 4-plate spectral gallery, an orbital split-screen comparator, normalized topographic profiles, regolith thermal inertia scales, a 24-hour diurnal temperature simulator, an 8-axis radar breakdown, where the analogy breaks down, and TRL 4–6 test protocols, alongside an evidence vault to download our 8 processed CSV datasets and export PDF/Markdown reports.

This tool helps mission planners select accurate terrestrial proving grounds while accounting for Earth’s physical limits.
details:
Project Links

Web App: https://autumn-solara.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Jack-Levi/Autumn-Solara

What Does Autumn Solara Do and How Does It Work?

Autumn Solara is an interactive web platform built to compare 14 terrestrial analog sites against four NASA lunar and Martian reference destinations:

1. Shackleton Crater (Lunar South Pole, Artemis III): Permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), illuminated rim peaks, and volatile cold traps.

2. Copernicus Crater (Lunar Mare Insularum): Complex impact crater with terraced walls, central peaks, and impact melt sheets.

3. Jezero Crater (Mars, Perseverance/Mars Sample Return): Ancient lacustrine and deltaic basin containing carbonates and phyllosilicates.

4. Alba Mons (Mars, Tharsis Volcanic Province): Low-angle shield volcano with collapsed calderas, lava tubes, and radial grabens.

When a user selects one of the four NASA destinations or adjusts mission weights, our client-side Planetary Fidelity Index (PFI) algorithm scores and orders all 14 Earth locations. The catalog pairs seven classic sites (Atacama Desert, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Haughton Crater on Devon Island, Barringer Crater, Río Tinto, Askja Highlands, and Mauna Kea/Kilauea) with seven additional candidates (Salar de Uyuni, Lanzarote Lava Tubes, El Pinacate Volcanic Field, Danakil Depression, Campo de Piedra Pómez, La Payunia Volcanic Reserve, and Lake Salda).

The web application contains five functional modules:

Eight-Dimension PFI Calibration System: Calculates compatibility scores across Geology and Mineralogy, Terrain and Slopes, Temperature and Illumination, Water/Ice and ISRU, Dust/Wind and Erosion, Biology and Extremophiles, Caves and Lava Tubes, and Robotic/Human Operations.

Global Map and Coordinate Inspector: A multi-layer Leaflet map displaying Optical Satellite (Esri), Topographic Relief (USGS SRTM), and Thermal layers, paired with an interactive coordinate tool that estimates elevation, slope, and PFI compatibility.

Multi-Gravity Rover Mobility Simulator: An interactive transect tool that calculates vehicle pitch (degrees), slope stability margins, regolith sinkage, and estimated traction power (W) across crater and volcanic profiles under Earth (9.81 m/s²), Martian (3.72 m/s²), and Lunar (1.62 m/s²) gravity.

Geological Case Studies (Six Analytical Sections per Site):

1. Scale, Process, and Optimal Homolog Notice: Displays spatial micro-scales and active geological processes, and alerts the user if another NASA destination in the catalog has a higher PFI match for that site.

2. Four-Plate Inspection Gallery: Displays a ground-level field photograph, a zenithal USGS SRTM 30m topographic map, a satellite orthoimage, and the corresponding NASA orbital image.

3. Zenithal Orbital Split-Screen Comparator and Reading Guide: A curtain slider comparing Earth satellite imagery against Moon/Mars orbital imagery, accompanied by a three-column guide explaining what features to look for on the left, on the right, and why the comparison matters.

4. Normalized Dual-Axis Topographic Profiles and Thermal Inertia Scales: Interactive SVG elevation profiles (SRTM 30m vs. LRO LOLA and MGS MOLA DEM) with a hover crosshair showing distance, elevation, slope, and relative relief (Δh), plus a regolith Thermal Inertia scale (TIU, J·m⁻²·K⁻¹·s⁻¹/²) based on MGS TES, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, and LRO Diviner data.

5. 24-Hour Diurnal Thermal Cycle (00:00h to 23:00h): An interactive hourly chart comparing terrestrial MODIS LST temperature curves against LRO Diviner (with selectable Artemis Illuminated Rim and 42 K Permanent Shadowed Region modes) and Martian TES/THEMIS cycles to visualize the thermal difference (ΔT).

6. Eight-Axis Radar Chart, Analogy Breakdown, and TRL 4-6 Protocols: Summarizes why each site matches, where the local analogy breaks down, Earth's four universal physical barriers, and suggested TRL 4-6 testing protocols.

Data Vault and Report Generator: Lets users preview and download the eight CSV datasets used in the project, view the 14-site justification table, and export a summary report in PDF or Markdown format.

WHAT FACTORS DID OUR TEAM CONSIDER?

Looking Beyond Famous Benchmarks: We included less common sites with strong geomorphic or mineralogical similarities, such as La Payunia for shield volcanism on Alba Mons, Lake Salda for hydromagnesite deltaic deposits in Jezero Crater, Campo de Piedra Pomez for wind-eroded yardangs, and El Pinacate for volcanic ash and maar craters.

Showing Where the Analogy Breaks Down: Because no location on Earth duplicates lunar or Martian environments completely, every site study lists local limitations (such as atmospheric moisture, rainfall, or vegetation) alongside four universal physical differences: gravity (0.165g and 0.379g), atmospheric pressure and vacuum (10⁻¹² Pa on the Moon; 6.1 hPa CO₂ on Mars), radiation, and unweathered regolith.

Relative Relief Normalization: Plotting raw elevations (such as +3,185 m on Earth and -1,715 m on the Moon) on a single axis flattens both curves. We normalized the SVG profiles using dual vertical axes so the actual shapes and slopes of the craters and volcanoes can be compared visually.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Before testing rovers, drills, ground-penetrating radars (GPR), or EVA suits in the field, teams need to know which terrestrial environment best represents their target destination and what environmental differences they must compensate for. Autumn Solara brings dispersed geological descriptions and orbital data into one accessible educational and planning interface, allowing users to compare sites side by side and download the underlying CSV tables and summary reports.

HOW IS THE PROJECT CREATIVE?

We designed the platform with a clean, monochrome editorial layout so the satellite imagery and charts remain the focus:

WebGL GLSL Liquid Cursor: We implemented a custom Framebuffer Object (FBO) shader with chromatic dispersion that reacts to mouse movement while keeping the center transparent so text and graphs remain readable.

Interactive Visual Tools: Instead of presenting static text pages, we turned the topographic transects, the 24-hour temperature comparison, the rover slope physics, and the satellite image comparisons into interactive components.

TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE USED

Frontend and Coding Languages: HTML5, CSS3, TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide Icons.

Graphics and Mapping: Custom WebGL/GLSL fragment and vertex shaders, interactive SVG charts, Leaflet.js, Esri World Imagery tiles, and USGS SRTM topographic tiles.

Data Preparation: Python scripts (fetch_and_create_datasets.py) used to prepare and structure our eight CSV datasets from NASA LRO LOLA, NASA LRO Diviner, NASA MGS MOLA and TES, NASA Mars Odyssey THEMIS, USGS/NASA SRTM 30m, ASTER, and NASA Earthdata MODIS, combined with open scientific literature and Wikimedia Commons imagery.

Hardware and Development Environment: Built on standard personal computers (Windows environment) using Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub, and AI coding assistants for shader math refinement and UI component structuring.
